new_statements.translation: The tonic accent plays an important role in Kiluba Hemba. If one displaces it, one risks not being understood, or saying things quite different from what one meant, for certain words, wholly alike in spelling, have totally different meanings according to the place given to the tonic accent. What is more, it very often happens that a word written the same way and bearing the same tonic accent differs in meaning according to whether the vowel of the syllable is long or short. Usage will certainly have to be the surest guide; however, [...] we shall give each word, as far as possible, its tonic accent

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position is given. The 'accent tonique' of Kiluba-hemba is lexically placed and distinctive: its position alone separates otherwise identical words, and vowel length is a second independent contrast. Colle (1913, tome II p. 661), the companion first-hand source, makes the phonetic nature explicit: every word carries an accent that 'is not the prosodic accent but the tonic, musical or acute accent', i.e. a raised pitch, and in trisyllables this high pitch falls either on the penult or on the antepenult depending on the word (lùbuzi 'big goat', bàluba vs kamùntu 'little man'), 'likewise for shorter and longer words'. Read together: Hemba is a tone (pitch accent-like) language whose word 'accent' is a lexically unpredictable high pitch, not a dynamic stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Colle says the same holds for shorter and longer words. Vandermeiren adds that vowel length (long vs short, marked grave vs acute in the dictionary) independently distinguishes words that bear the same accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: Vandermeiren gives 'à chaque mot.. son accent tonique' (dictionary citation forms, accent marked with acute on short vowels and grave on long vowels); Colle: 'Chaque mot comporte un accent'. Colle's second-hand-free supporting quote (tome II, p. 661, file): 'Chaque mot comporte un accent, qui n'est pas l'accent prosodique, mais l'accent tonique, musical, ou aigu. Ces trois derniers mots désignent cette même inflexion élevée (le do aigu). Voici un mot de trois syllabes; il possède deux sons graves et un son aigu; le son aigu frappe soit la pénultième, soit l'antipénultième; on dira, par exemple : lùbuzi (une grande chèvre), bàluba, avec l'accent aigu sur lù et sur bà; ou bien kamùntu (un petit homme), avec l'accent aigu sur mù.' The 1912 grammar (not opened) presumably has the fuller treatment.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Kiluba-hemba of the 'Baluba de l'est' / Baluba-Hemba of the Urua (Buluba-hemba) between the Lualaba and Lake Tanganyika (White Fathers' mission area, Kongolo–Kiambi), i.e. Hemba proper (hemb1242, Guthrie L.34), not Yazi or Zeela; the example forms show the Hemba h-reflex (kihona 'chair', ha-nzibo 'at the house') where Luba-Katanga has p. Vandermeiren's 1913 dictionary and 1912 grammar are the works Glottolog cites for hemb1242; Colle's monograph is the ethnography of the same population and defers to Vandermeiren for the language.

sources.note: Introduction §V, p. 11: 'l'accent tonique' plays an important role in kiluba hemba; moving it changes the meaning, since words identical in spelling differ in meaning by the place of the accent tonique; vowel length is also distinctive; the dictionary marks each word's accent (acute = short vowel, grave = long vowel). No fixed position stated.

sources.note: p. 661: 'Chaque mot comporte un accent, qui n'est pas l'accent prosodique, mais l'accent tonique, musical, ou aigu' (a high-pitch inflexion); in a trisyllable the high pitch falls either on the penult or the antepenult (lùbuzi, bàluba vs kamùntu), likewise for shorter and longer words; p. 662 adds long/semi-long/short syllable length as a second basis of drum language. Refers the reader to Vandermeiren's grammar and dictionary for details.
